newsitem.title: JAPAN: Corporate sentiment still not impoved in Osaka - BOJ.
newsitem.headline: Corporate sentiment still not impoved in Osaka - BOJ.

text.p: Production has clearly picked up in western Japan's Kansai region, but corporate sentiment has still not shown an improvement due to concern about the economic outlook for the next fiscal year, the Bank of Japan's (BOJ) Osaka branch manager Eiichiro Kinoshita said on Monday.

Kinoshita told a news conference on the first day of a BOJ branch managers' meeting that the recent plunge in Tokyo stock prices had confirmed that financial markets and companies were concerned about the outlook for the economy.
"Of course, the plunge in stock prices may strengthen concern (among companies) about the economic outlook," said Kinoshita, who is also a BOJ executive director.

"There is concern about the possible effects of the stock market plunge on private consumption...But we cannot tell in precise terms how it will affect consumption as we have not had sufficient discussions with employers yet," he said.
"Production has picked up in the second half of this fiscal year, but in comparison, corporate sentiment has not improved much," he said.
He added that there was a "gap" between the state of the economy and corporate sentiment.

Kinoshita said that although production was likely to remain on an upward trend for the rest of the current fiscal year to March 31, uncertainty over fiscal factors such as a planned rise of the consumption tax from three percent to five percent from April 1 was keeping businesses cautious.
He also said that increased competition had forced firms to keep prices low and this was eating away at their profits.
However, Kinoshita said bleak corporate sentiment would not lead to a worsening of the economy.
"This cautious attitude will not lead to a shrinkage of companies' economic activity," he said.
"The region's economy is gradually recovering and gaining firmness."
Kinoshita said the recent depreciation of the yen had only boosted profits to a limited extent because of price competition.
But he added that the yen's weakening had helped lift production as it had slowed down plans by the region's firms to move production overseas.
The yen's appreciation against the dollar up to mid-1995 prompted Japanese manufacturers to shift production overseas to avoid higher costs in Japan.

"Although firms have not altered their long-term strategy of shifting production abroad, the recent weakness of the yen has slowed that process down and has led some to keep production facilities in the country.
"This has had a big effect in pushing up production," Kinoshita said.
